clue.text: Fifty cent cut is a big lump!

parts.note: fifty cents is half a dollar, and half of the word dollar is DOL
to lop is to cut off

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a fifty-cent coin, once cut, makes a surprisingly hefty chunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifty cent' is half a dollar, so take half the word DOLLAR, its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollop is a shapeless mass or large spoonful of something soft.

clue.text: Some decorator I offered work depicting Bible story

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A painter-decorator offers up a piece of work showing a scene from Scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: An oratorio is a large musical composition for voices, usually setting a sacred text, as Handel's Messiah does.

clue.text: Navigational aid at sea so led sailor

indicators.note: being at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor at sea steered his course by some guiding device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' turns SO LED into LODES; TAR is the usual crossword sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodestar is a guiding star, such as the Pole Star, used by sailors to steer by.

clue.text: Element of safeguard in theatre

definitions.meaning: a chemical element, a silvery metal of the platinum group
a protection, from the statue of Pallas that was said to keep Troy safe
a famous London variety theatre bears this name

explanation.surface: Asks what part of a theatre's security arrangements is fundamental.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: the metal, a safeguard (after the protective image of Pallas at Troy), and the London Palladium, a well-known theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a metallic element, a protective charm, and a renowned London music-hall venue.

clue.text: Bishop, for one, requiring church to get manses renovated

indicators.note: something renovated has been made over, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bishop needs the church to refurbish the ministers' houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bishop' tempts towards the clergy alongside church and manses, but it is the chess piece; 'renovated' gives ESSMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop is one of the pieces in chess, an example of the general term.

clue.text: Acton let brother wrong her sister Currer

indicators.note: to set something wrong is to put it awry, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Acton allowed a brother to do her sister Currer an injustice.
explanation.walkthrough: Acton, Currer and Ellis Bell were the pen names of Anne, Charlotte and Emily; 'her' points back to Acton, so the sister called Currer is wanted. 'wrong' rearranges ACTON LET BROTHER.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist who wrote Jane Eyre published under the pseudonym Currer Bell, and Anne (Acton Bell) was her younger sibling.

clue.text: Drink wine — Bordeaux, say

parts.note: the drink is slang for the sea
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Someone orders a glass of wine, perhaps a claret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bordeaux' looks like the wine; it is the French port city. 'the drink' is informal for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Bordeaux is a harbour city on the Garonne, an example of a coastal trading town.

clue.text: Like one's life in a prior existence?

definitions.text: Like one's life in a prior existence?

parts.words: Like one's life in a prior existence?
parts.note: seems to ask about a past life, but a prior is a senior monk, so it describes life in a religious house

explanation.surface: A question about what one's past life might have been like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prior' reads as earlier; here it is the head of a priory.
explanation.definitionFit: Life under a prior is the cloistered life of monks.

clue.text: Muses over beer-casks people in pub aim to down

definitions.text: people in pub aim to down

indicators.note: in a down clue, over says the first piece sits on top of the next

parts.note: there were nine Muses in Greek myth
a pin is a small beer cask holding four and a half gallons

explanation.surface: The Muses ponder beer barrels that drinkers in a pub mean to drink up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down' suggests drinking; here it means knock over, as in skittles.
explanation.definitionFit: Skittles in a pub game are set up for players to knock over with a ball.

clue.text: Beach jumper

parts.note: looks like a sweater worn at the seaside, but describes a small hopping creature of the shore

explanation.surface: A sweater for the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' is British for a sweater; here it is something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny crustacean lives among seaweed on the shore and leaps about like an insect.

clue.text: Gun shot, hitting two targets in succession

definitions.text: shot, hitting two targets in succession
definitions.meaning: in billiards, a stroke where the cue ball strikes two balls one after the other

explanation.surface: A gunshot that hits two targets one after another.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a big artillery gun and a billiards stroke striking two balls in turn.

clue.text: This type of grass plagues late batsmen

parts.note: to dog someone is to plague or pursue them
in cricket the tail is the weaker batsmen who come in last

explanation.surface: A grass that troubles the lower-order batsmen in cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' hints at cricket slang for informing; it is the plant. In cricket the 'tail' is the last few batsmen, usually poor at batting.
explanation.definitionFit: Crested dogstail is a common meadow grass named for its spike-like flower head.

clue.text: Playing football, the means that justifies the ends?

definitions.text: Playing football, the means that justifies the ends?

parts.words: Playing football, the means that justifies the ends?
parts.note: twists the saying about ends justifying means: before a football match a coin flip decides which end each team defends

explanation.surface: A twist on the moral saying that the end justifies the means, set in football.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ends' are the two halves of the pitch, decided by spinning a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Flipping a coin at kick-off settles which end each side plays towards.

clue.text: Searching, check in drug trial

parts.note: acid is slang for the drug LSD
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: A thorough investigation into a drug's clinical trial.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Searching check', the comma only a surface pause.
explanation.definitionFit: A decisive, rigorous examination of worth, from testing gold with nitric acid.

clue.text: Misses being secure, beset by dreadful stress

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded, so the secure word goes inside the other letters
dreadful marks the word stress as badly treated, so its letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
to pin is to secure or fasten

explanation.surface: Young women anxious about safety are terribly stressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misses' looks like a verb (fails to hit) but is the plural of Miss; 'dreadful' gives SSTERS, which 'beset by' wraps round the fastening word.
explanation.definitionFit: Misses is a title for unmarried women, which is what the plural noun denotes.

clue.text: Audibly disapprove of king who has bad manners?

parts.note: to boo is to show disapproval out loud
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Crowd jeering at a monarch with poor etiquette.
explanation.definitionFit: A lout or churl is someone ill-mannered and coarse.

clue.text: Puffed up account due to be paid

parts.note: a bill is an account of money owed
owed means still to be paid

explanation.surface: An overdue bill that has been inflated.
explanation.definitionFit: Sails or smoke that swelled out in great waves are said to have bulged and puffed.

clue.text: Note bid East contrived — it is biddable

indicators.note: contrived means artificially arranged, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bridge player notes the bid East has engineered, and finds it easily led.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it is' is a link. 'bid' and 'East' suggest bridge; 'contrived' rearranges NOTE, BID and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Biddable describes someone docile and willing to do as told.

clue.text: Plays part or play parts

definitions.meaning: performs a role or behaves in a certain way
the main divisions of a stage drama

explanation.surface: Performs a role, or the sections of a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means performs a role; the noun means the main divisions of a drama.

clue.text: Mention initial change needed in conjuring trick

indicators.note: says the first letter of the following word is to be swapped for another

parts.note: an illusion is a magician's trick

explanation.surface: A magician says his trick needs a small tweak at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initial change' replaces the first letter, I, of ILLUSION with A.
explanation.definitionFit: An allusion is an indirect reference to something.

clue.text: Without spades, coppice gets densely planted

indicators.note: here without means outside, so the coppice goes round the spades

parts.note: a thicket is a coppice or dense growth of trees
S is the card-game abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A thicket, cleared without spades, becomes overgrown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking; here it is the old sense outside, so THICKET goes round S.
explanation.definitionFit: Thickset means set closely together, as dense planting is; it also describes a stocky build.

clue.text: Put in danger about first of April? August, actually

indicators.note: about means around, so the danger word goes round the letter

parts.note: to imperil is to put in danger

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone frets that early April is risky, but then it is really August.
explanation.walkthrough: 'August' looks like the month; it is the adjective meaning majestic. 'actually' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: August as an adjective means grand and dignified, like an emperor.

clue.text: Mendelssohn's fourth vermouth?

definitions.meaning: Mendelssohn's Symphony No 4 has a nickname from the country that inspired it
sweet red vermouth is often called by its country of origin, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: Did Mendelssohn's fourth symphony come with a cocktail?
explanation.definitionFit: Mendelssohn's Fourth Symphony is named for Italy, and sweet vermouth from Italy is ordered by that national name.

clue.text: Abused lady in ancient language

indicators.note: abused means misused or ill-treated, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman mistreated in an old tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abused' rearranges LADY into LYDIA, followed by IN.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue of Lydia, an Iron Age kingdom of western Anatolia, is extinct.

clue.text: R. Crusoe, wrecked, needs energy and initiative

indicators.note: wrecked suggests the castaway's ship, and signals the letters broken up

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Robinson Crusoe, shipwrecked, must be energetic and enterprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' rearranges R CRUSOE into RESOURC, then E.
explanation.definitionFit: Resource in the singular can mean ingenuity or the ability to find ways out of difficulty.

clue.text: Small, nasty, tailless beetle

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small

indicators.note: tailless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: vile means nasty

explanation.surface: A small, unpleasant beetle that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' drops the last letter of VILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A weevil is a small beetle with a long snout, a pest of grain.

clue.text: . The most destitute perish in teens, tragically

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the other
tragically suggests events gone badly wrong, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written
to perish is to die

explanation.surface: The poorest people die young, which is tragic.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray full stop before the clue is a printing mark; 'tragically' gives NEEST, which 'in' wraps round the word for perish.
explanation.definitionFit: The poorest are the people in greatest want.

clue.text: Set off in point-to point included in meeting

indicators.note: included in means placed inside, so these letters go within the meeting word

parts.note: a date is an arranged meeting
E, east, is a compass point
taken as written
N, north, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A bomb goes off at a cross-country horse race during a race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point-to-point' looks like a horse race; it is a compass point, TO, and another point.
explanation.definitionFit: To detonate is to explode or set off a charge.

clue.text: Political body injecting constituency with new energy

indicators.note: injecting puts one piece inside another, here the new letter into the constituency

parts.note: a seat is a parliamentary constituency
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A legislature brings fresh vigour to a voting district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injecting' puts N into SEAT, giving SENAT, then E follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A senate is a legislative assembly or upper house.
